newsitem.title: FRANCE: France plans overhaul of state sector supervision.
newsitem.headline: France plans overhaul of state sector supervision.

text.p: France's centre-right government, bidding to show the public sector will be in safer hands with it than with the opposition Socialist party, announced on Wednesday an overhaul of the way it supervises state-owned companies.

The reform will include privatisations where possible, and more professional supervision for companies which remain in state hands -- including bringing in experts from the private sector -- to prevent a repeat of the massive losses run up by state companies in the past.
Finance Minister Jean Arthuis, presenting a "reform of the role of the state as shareholder", told a news conference it was meant to make the mistakes of the past impossible.

Among these were state bank Credit Lyonnais, allowed by the previous Socialist government to embark on a spending spree which left the incoming centre-right government with a hefty bill to pick up its subsequent losses.
The reform will set up a new council attached to the finance ministry, headed by someone from the private sector, to supervise the state's involvement in state-owned companies.

It also aims to sharpen the role of state representatives on the boards of public sector companies, ensure greater transparency in state company accounts and step up supervision of shell companies set up to carry bad loans hived off from state companies including Credit Lyonnais.

It will be followed by a reform of France's powerful Treasury to separate out the state's functions as shareholder and regulator to prevent any conflict of interest. Full details of the reform of the Treasury have yet to be announced.
Arthuis denied that there was any connection between the decision to announce the reform on Wednesday and the forthcoming two-round parliamentary election on May 25 and June 1.
But the centre-right nonetheless seized on the opportunity to snipe at the Socialist party's record in government between 1988 and 1993.

"It is because (the state's) duties were not respected in the past that the public sector has faced financial disasters which brought incomprehension and indignation among our people and which introduced doubts about the state's ability to manage public services," government spokesman Alain Lamassoure quoted President Jacques Chirac as telling a cabinet meeting.
"It was particularly during the 1988-1993 period that the most serious misadventures happened. We have seen dangerous strategies, dissimulation, poor control and short-sighted managers," Chirac said.

The Socialist party has tried to make preservation of France's large state sector an election issue by promising to halt new privatisations, including the partial sale due next month of France Telecom.
But the centre-right, though pledging to continue state sales, has stopped well short of the free-market sell all approach called for by some on the most liberal wing of the ruling coalition.
Arthuis said the state had a responsibility to ensure sound management both for companies not yet ready for privatisation and for those essential public services which would remain in state hands.
